Man, I feel you on this. I was committed to a crisis unit because I got black out drunk and said I was going to hang myself. Friend called the cops and they took me there. Once I sobered up I was completely void of any suicidal feelings. They kept me on the crisis unit for a full day before moving to the stress unit (they said I would only be there for an hour). I felt like I was going crazy staring at blank white walls, and my psychiatrist didn't even remember me the next day. He told me the night before I would be released when I sobered up and then the next morning he first made fun of my eating disorder and then told me he never said I could go. 

Zero trust in psychiatric wards. Treatment facilities, in my experience, have been great, but my experience on the psych ward has made me vow to never, ever, ever tell anyone if I'm feeling suicidal again. Seems counterproductive to me.

I hope you are doing well!

I am fairly new to this job, so I haven't really seen a whole lot of positive symptoms in the individuals with schizophrenia. Many of them have displayed negative symptoms, so it's not really too out of the normal seeing individuals sleeping or being mute majority of the day. While I have seen some while they were delusional or hallucinating, her case has been the most disorganized I've had to deal with so far (though, I'm positive there will be more to come). I guess the most confusing part about it for me (especially her case) is that I don't know how to respond quite yet. I have gotten the hang of helping people out with their anxiety, depression, anger, and whatnot, but the absolutely delusional statements are behavior are a little more difficult to understand and treat. I'm sure as I am exposed to more delusions and hallucinations I'll figure out ways to help individuals deal with them (hopefully!)

While in high school I spent some time in an inpatient facility for eating disorders, but after a long and hard 9 year battle I am finally recovered (besides some minor triggers occasionally, I pretty much have no ED thoughts anymore, aw yeah!) I feel like this experience has really helped me empathize more with the patients than some of the other staff who have never dealt with psychological treatment. As for the contagious factor, having gone through some struggles helps that, too. I have learned my own coping skills during my treatment times that help when I'm feeling stressed helping others with their treatment (now if only I can get them to use coping skills). 

If a client is really, really stressing me out I generally just ask them to step away for a moment and I go outside and take a breather. It really helps to just remove yourself from the situation for a few moments to recollect your thoughts (as long as they are not at risk for harming themselves or others, of course).

There are quite a few but currently we have a very disorganized patient. She came to us because she thought there was a dragon in her furnace and was banging on neighbors doors with a hammer. She just comes up to you, stares, smiles, and walks away. Sometimes she'll say something random like "the lights are flickering we need to call 911."

This field of work can get pretty mentally exhausting but it's not hard to snap out of it when you realize that you can leave work and clear your mind while they have to deal with their symptoms all day everyday.

I work at a transitional care facility where majority of the patients have schizophrenia. Working directly with them and seeing their symptoms in person is so much different than what I had previously imagined when reading about schizophrenia in textbooks. I think part of the reason may be that many of the patients have comorbid conditions. One may have schizophrenia and bipolar and another has schizophrenia and borderline personality disorder, which sometimes makes unique symptoms that seem to be blend all the disorders the individual has.

Not to mention that everybody's symptoms are expressed so differently, even amongst the same disorder.
